steps.do: Before you start: set CALIBER_FEATURE_ARIA=true on the CALIBER server and restart it; Aria and the Plans page are off by default. Open Aria's planner. Click Plans in the left sidebar (under the Integrations group; the page carries a Preview badge). This opens the Aria Plans page, where you hand Aria a one-line goal and it decomposes it into platform steps you approve before anything runs.
steps.see: The Aria Plans page with a Goal textarea, an Autonomy selector, and a Decompose goal button.

steps.do: State the intent. Paste the canonical one-line intent from intent.md into the Goal field. The exact wording matters: the default planner keys off the literal domain words judge and eval dataset, so keep both in the sentence (it also recognises "test set" for the dataset step, but a phrase like "faithfulness scoring" would not produce a judge step). Set Autonomy to Stop before each change (this is the ask_each level) so Aria asks you to approve every mutate step.
fill: Create a judge for answer faithfulness and an eval dataset to run it on.
steps.see: A draft plan appears below the form.

steps.do: Review the decomposed plan. Confirm Aria produced exactly two steps from the one sentence — judge.create and eval_dataset.create — matching expected-plan.json. This decomposition is the autonomous-orchestration showcase: one intent in, the right governed steps out.
steps.see: The draft plan lists two mutate steps: judge.create and eval_dataset.create.

steps.do: Approve the plan shape. With the plan in draft status, click Approve plan. This records that you accept the orchestration before any step runs.
steps.see: The plan moves to approved status and an Execute button appears.

steps.do: Execute the plan. Click Execute. Aria reaches the first step, judge.create, but the planner could not know the judge's name or instructions, so it pauses on a violet Aria needs information form: "Provide the required inputs for step 1: Create judge." with a field per capability input (name and instructions are marked required) and two buttons, Continue plan and Skip step.
steps.see: The plan pauses on the judge.create step (WAITING INPUT) with an Aria needs information form.
steps.asset: Plan running, paused at the judge.create input form

steps.do: Fill the form with the judge spec from answer-faithfulness.judge.json — these are the judge.create inputs. The instructions must reference {{ inputs }} / {{ outputs }} / {{ expectations }} (at least one is required); set feedback value type to bool. Click Continue plan: Aria merges and validates the inputs (a bad value is rejected and the form stays open), then — because autonomy is ask_each — raises an Aria needs your approval prompt, "Approve step 1: Create judge (judge.create)?".
fill:
You audit whether an assistant answer is faithful to its evidence. You are given the request {{ inputs }}, the model {{ outputs }}, and the reference {{ expectations }}.

Return true ONLY if every factual claim in {{ outputs }} is supported by {{ expectations }} (or by evidence cited in {{ inputs }}), and the answer makes no unsupported commitments. If any claim is unsupported, contradicted, or hallucinated, return false. Judge faithfulness only — not style.
your configured judge model (e.g. the gateway default)
steps.see: The form closes and a pending Approve / Deny prompt for judge.create appears.

steps.do: Click Approve — Aria runs judge.create and the plan moves on to eval_dataset.create. That step has nothing to ask: the planner linked its name to the judge step's name, so it raises only an Approve / Deny prompt. Click Approve again; Aria creates an empty versioned test set (named AnswerFaithfulness, taken from the judge step) and the plan reaches completed. (Deny would mark a step skipped instead.)
steps.see: Both steps show DONE and the plan status is COMPLETED.
steps.asset: Plan completed (judge + test set created by Aria)

steps.where: Agent resources › Judges  +  Prompt lifecycle › Test Sets  +  Integrations › Plans
steps.do: Verify the end-to-end result. Confirm three things: Judges shows AnswerFaithfulness active with Returns = bool; Test Sets shows an empty test set AnswerFaithfulness at version 1; and the Plans page shows the plan completed with both steps done. Together these prove Aria turned one sentence into a governed two-step plan and created the two real artifacts. (For a separately named set, create one on Test Sets from support-faithfulness.dataset.json.)
steps.see: An active judge, a real test set, and a completed two-step plan — the scenario gate.
steps.asset: Verified judge + test set + completed plan

steps.do: (Follow-up) Put the harness to work. Add example rows to the new AnswerFaithfulness test set — either author them in the row editor at /eval-datasets/:id → + Add example, or in Observability open a trace, use its Add to test set panel, pick the test set under Choose test set, and click Add example (or reuse a starter dataset such as cookbooks/01-prompt-regression-lab/assets/dataset/). Then go to Evaluations, click Run evaluation, pick the test set, tick the built-in Graders, and tick your AnswerFaithfulness judge under Custom LLM judges so it runs as a Judge.<id> scorer for an automatic per-row verdict. This is the same scored-run loop as SCN-01 / SCN-10 and needs a real model provider — the default evaluator and LLM are fake, and Run evaluation returns a 400 without one.
fill: built-in scorers (Contains expected, Token F1, Non-empty) + AnswerFaithfulness under Custom LLM judges
steps.see: A scorecard run grades the rows on the deterministic scorers plus the AnswerFaithfulness judge column, closing the loop from one intent to a running evaluation harness.
steps.asset: (follow-up) Scored run + AnswerFaithfulness judge verdicts using the Aria-built harness
